paper_title: Antom 3-in-1 Transformer: A Payment Foundation Model

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: We report the development of Antom 3-in-1 Transformer, a payment foundation model that integrates sequence, tabular, and graph representations for payment risk detection. The model contains approximately 7B parameters, with approximately 1.7B activated per task route. Antom 3-in-1 Transformer is pretrained to learn reusable behavioral and relational representations, primarily on Ant International's internal payment data. In a cross-business transfer experiment, pretraining improves the target business metric by 34.5% over the same architecture trained from scratch. With only 25% of the training labels, the pretrained model outperforms the full-label scratch baseline in Average Precision (AP) and Recall@0.5% on different merchant domains. In a four-month online experiment on Ant International's billion-scale payment platform, the model reduced the overall loss rate by 37.88% relative to XGB-Online.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Large-scale payment platforms need to continuously detect fraud across different markets and business scenarios. Ant International has accumulated substantial transaction data and experience in risk prevention as its business has expanded. Antom, brand of Ant International, is unified merchant payment and digitalisation platform serving businesses of all sizes across Asia and worldwide. User behavior, transaction processes, and data distributions differ across scenarios, while fraudsters continually adjust their tactics and create new forms of risk (He et al., 2026). These changes increase the work required to maintain effective risk systems across markets. They motivate transaction foundation model that generalizes across scenarios and tactics and supports the continued prevention of complex payment risks. Research on transaction foundation models has made substantial progress (Han et al., 2026; Zuo et al., 2026). TransactionGPT learns transaction trajectories through autoregressive modeling and 1 combines transaction metadata with downstream features (Dou et al., 2025). PRAGMA uses masked reconstruction to learn transferable representations from heterogeneous banking events and user attributes. PANTHER combines generative pretraining with contrastive learning and applies behavioral representations to business decisions (Li et al., 2025). These approaches develop rich representations of individual histories. Payment risk also depends on relationships across accounts and payment objects. In its anti-money-laundering analysis, PRAGMA identifies the difficulty of capturing highly relational patterns through independent history encoding (Ostroukhov et al., 2026). The same transaction can also present different signals from different perspectives: an ordinary-looking user history may coexist with an associated network location or device that carries high-risk context. Jointly modeling these perspectives gives risk assessment more complete transaction context (Jiang et al., 2026). Based on these observations, we propose Antom 3-in-1 Transformer, foundation model for cardpayment risk that integrates transaction sequences, scenario-specific tabular features, and entity relationships. It has approximately 7B total parameters, with approximately 1.7B activated for single task route. The model combines behavioral histories, transaction fields, and user relations that specialized risk models often process separately. Large-scale pretraining learns transaction behavior and entity relations; business adaptation connects this knowledge to the objectives and decision rules of each business. The resulting foundation supports cross-scenario reuse, learning with limited labels, and behavioral analysis. In transfer experiment, adapting an existing source-domain foundation to new business improves the business metric by 34.5% over the same architecture trained from scratch. With only 25% of the training labels, the pretrained model outperforms the full-label scratch baseline in Average Precision (AP) and Recall@0.5% on both merchant domains. shared-checkpoint study evaluates adaptation across Antom-Merchant A, Antom-Merchant and AlipayHK. Pretrained representations also distinguish evasion and account-nurturing behavior. These studies examine the reusable behavioral capabilities contributed by pretraining. Joint-model comparisons then show how behavioral and relational information improves risk detection when combined with scenario features. In production, Antom 3-in-1 Transformer reduces overall loss rate by 37.88% relative to XGB-Online at the same 0.5% intervention budget.

sections.title: 2 Scope and Limitations of this Technical Report
sections.content: This report focuses on the adaptation capabilities, label efficiency, and industrial deployment of Antom 3-in-1 Transformer. The model is pretrained through sequence contrastive learning and self-supervised learning for graph relationship, respectively, primarily on Ant Internationals internal payment data. Subsequent supervised fine-tuning adapts the model to scenario-specific risk objectives across Antom and other Ant International businesses. We are committed to independent auditing of our technologies and have shared initial findings and selected methodological details on payment foundation models in research papers accompanying this release. Detailed model architecture, training configurations, and dataset construction procedures are outside the scope of this release. We briefly introduce the model architecture and pretraining method here. We plan to make further technical details available to additional third parties who can advise us on how to weigh the competitive and safety considerations above against the scientific value of further transparency. 2 Figure 1 Overview of Antom 3-in-1 Transformer. (a) Sequence modality. Independent Transformer towers encode user, card, and device histories. (b) Tabular modality. Field attention captures interactions among transaction attributes and business features. (c) Graph modality. graph attention network combines account profiles and rolling user graphs to learn relational representations. (d) Task-conditioned fusion. Task queries and sparse experts fuse sequence and tabular representations; graph embeddings augment the risk head.

sections.title: 3 Methodology Overview
sections.content: We introduce Antom 3-in-1 Transformer, payment foundation model that integrates sequence, tabular, and graph representations for payment risk detection. Figure 1 presents the architecture of Antom 3-in-1 Transformer. The sequence modality learns behavioral patterns from transaction histories. The tabular modality models interactions among transaction attributes, business states, and engineered features through self-attention. The graph modality captures relationships among users by aggregating their profile and connected neighborhoods . Each modality has corresponding encoder. Task-conditioned fusion combines sequence, tabular and graph representations for each prediction task. Sequence Encoder. The sequence encoder models the transaction histories associated with the current payment. Event tokenizer embeds each event through its amount, categorical fields, and elapsed time, then uses transformer to summarize the history. User, card, and device histories follow this procedure with separate encoders. The sequence encoders are pretrained by prefix-future contrast, which matches each historical prefix with statistical summary of its subsequent activity. Contrastive candidates with similar coarse activity profiles encourage the encoder to learn finer behavioral differences without risk labels. Tabular Encoder. The tabular encoder embeds features commonly used in payment-risk assessment, including current-transaction attributes and business statistics. The modeling procedure of tabular modality includes two stages: field tokenization embeds each value, and field interaction uses self-attention to combine information across fields. The resulting representations describe both individual fields and the transaction as whole. 3 Graph Encoder. The graph encoder models users through their account profiles and their connections to other users. We construct rolling user graphs from transactions in dynamic time interval. Each user node initializes from an embedding of its account. The graph encoder is pretrained by combining contrastive agreement between edge-perturbed views of the same user with reconstruction of relation counts. The objectives preserve neighborhood consistency and relational information without supervision. Task-Conditioned Fusion. For task-conditioned fusion, the model is optimized for paymentrisk prediction task together with set of auxiliary business tasks. We associate each task with learnable vector, referred to as task query. Learnable task queries aggregate information through shared attention, and the resulting task representations are used for expert routing. Downstream fine-tuning adapts Antom 3-in-1 Transformer to supervised risk and auxiliary tasks. It updates the sequence encoder and trains the tabular encoder, task-conditioned fusion module, experts, and prediction heads. The graph encoder is frozen and supplies user representations aligned with each transactions time.

sections.title: 4 Experiments
sections.content: We evaluate Antom 3-in-1 Transformer through overall risk-prediction performance, production deployment, and reuse across businesses and tasks. We then examine sequence pretraining, graph pretraining, task-conditioned fusion, followed by modality ablations and behavioral case studies.

sections.title: 4.1 Experimental Setup
sections.content: Datasets. We use five groups of datasets as follows. Industrial datasets. We use sampled card-payment transactions from multiple business scenarios at Ant International. Each transaction has tabular features, user/card/device sequences, and user graph information. IBM dataset. IBMs synthetic credit-card dataset (Padhi et al., 2021) contains 24,386,900 transactions. Low-label and cross-scenario datasets. These card-payment transaction datasets are sampled from core business of Ant International, including Antom-Merchant A, Antom-Merchant B, and AlipayHK (HK). Antom-Merchant represents global e-marketplace, while Antom-Merchant is pooled cohort of merchants spanning e-commerce, digital entertainment, travel and aviation, AI services, and other industries. AlipayHK is another important business for Ant International. Table 10 summarizes the three evaluation domains. Graph datasets. Amazon and YelpChi are multi-relation review graphs (Dou et al., 2020), TFinance is financial transaction graph (Tang et al., 2022), and Elliptic is Bitcoin transactionflow graph (Weber et al., 2019). Their statistics appear in Table 11. Fusion datasets. We use Sampled Industrial, TransXion, IBM CCT, and MBD. Appendix B.1 describes their inputs and splits  (Table 12)  . Baselines. Online risk prediction compares Antom 3-in-1 Transformer with XGB-Online (Chen and Guestrin, 2016) and the SAINT-style production model (Somepalli et al., 2021). Public transaction baselines include FATA-Trans, TabBERT-LSTM, PANTHER, TransactionGPT, and 4 PRAGMA (Dou et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025; Ostroukhov et al., 2026; Padhi et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2023b). Sequence pretraining compares PFC with CoLES, BYB, and CPC (Babaev et al., 2022; van den Oord et al., 2018; Wu et al., 2025), alongside training from scratch. Graph augmentation comparisons include tabular-only and graph-only models, concatenation, graph-token fusion, logit stacking, and residual predictors. Fusion comparisons use fixed model reference (denoted as B1), score-only fusion (denoted as B2), concatenation, sum-pooling, and learned fusion methods: CE, MMT, UMI, 𝐼 2𝑀 2, MMPareto, 𝐼 2MoE, and BALM (Gabeur et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2019; Madaan et al., 2024; Nguyen et al., 2026; Wei and Hu, 2024; Xin et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2023a). Model and comparison settings. The industrial configuration contains approximately 6.92B parameters, with approximately 1.74B activated per task route. Sequence pretraining objectives are compared using common encoder, pretraining data, and training budget. Graph and fusion comparisons follow their respective matched evaluation protocols. Metrics. We evaluate ranking quality offline with three metrics and business impact online with two loss rates. Average precision (AP) summarizes precision over the risk ranking. AUROC measures class separation across score thresholds. Top-budget recall R@𝑞 is the share of risk events captured among the highest-scoring 𝑞 fraction of transactions; we emphasize R@0.5%, the production intervention budget. Graph benchmarks report AUPRC (Tang et al., 2023). For online assessment, the amount-based chargeback (CB) rate divides chargeback amount by successful transaction amount. The overall loss rate uses the same denominator and counts the realized financial loss after chargeback-dispute recoveries. Appendix defines supplementary metrics.

sections.title: 4.2 Performance Overview
sections.content: We assess overall performance in two settings: Industrial online A/B test against the previous risk models; Open-source comparison with other pretrained models and transaction foundation models. Industrial Online A/B test. From June 8 to October 14, 2026, the online evaluation covered 30% of platform transactions. Transactions were randomly assigned to Antom 3-in-1 Transformer and two production models: XGB-Online, which periodically refits gradient-boosted trees, and the SAINT-style model. The three arms used the same business policies and intervention budget. Across the evaluated payment businesses, Antom 3-in-1 Transformer reduces the pooled CB rate by 37.74% and the overall loss rate by 37.88% relative to XGB-Online  (Table 1)  . Relative to SAINT-style, the reductions are 28.26% and 24.07%. Table 1 Online portfolio results relative to XGB-Online. System XGB-Online SAINT-style Antom 3-in-1 Transformer Traffic share 32.1% 37.4% 30.4% CB rate change base 13.21% 37.74% Loss rate change base 18.18% 37.88% The online Antom 3-in-1 Transformer was evaluated in two stages. In Stage (June 8August 2), all three arms scored traffic without intervening. Subsequent confirmed outcomes measure each arms 5 recall among its top 0.5% of scores. In Stage II (August 3October 14), each arm made production decisions under the same policies and 0.5% intervention budget, and we compare the realized CB rates. Financial outcomes include records received through October 25, 2026. In Stage I, Antom 3-in-1 Transformer recalls 29.79% of risk transactions, compared with 7.39% for XGB-Online and 16.52% for SAINT-style. In Stage II, its CB rate is 28.28% lower than that of XGBOnline; weighting the arms by common distribution of transaction dates gives 26.09% reduction  (Table 2)  . Stronger risk ranking thus translates into lower realized losses under the deployed intervention policy. Appendix B.2 specifies the transaction-date aggregation. Table 2 Two-stage card-payment evaluation. Stage II reports CB-rate results relative to XGBOnline. System XGB-Online SAINT-style Antom 3-in-1 Transformer Stage R@0.5% 7.39% 16.52% 29.79% Pooled base -12.66% -28.28% Stage II Date-weighted base -12.49% -26.09% Open-source comparison results. On the temporal test split of IBMs synthetic credit-card dataset, we compare Antom 3-in-1 Transformer with baseline configurations from five published approaches  (Table 3)  . Antom 3-in-1 Transformer achieves the highest reported AP, AUROC, R@0.5%, and R@1% among the evaluated configurations. Its AP of 0.3829 exceeds PRAGMAs 0.3412 by 12.2% on relative basis. At the 0.5% and 1% intervention budgets, Antom 3-in-1 Transformer recalls 83.22% and 97.17% of fraud, compared to 72.12% and 80.67% for PRAGMA, corresponding to increases of 11.10 and 16.50 percentage points. Antom 3-in-1 Transformer also attains the highest AUROC of 0.9966, compared with the five evaluated baselines. sections.title: 4.3 Industrial Implementation
sections.content: Antom 3-in-1 Transformer runs inside Ant Internationals real-time risk-control workflow. Every card payment triggers one scoring request: the feature platform assembles the model inputs, GPU model service computes the risk score, and the strategy platform turns the score into decision. The sequence and tabular encoders, task-conditioned fusion, and experts run online for each request, whereas graph embeddings are computed offline and only looked up at scoring time. Online system. payment event first enters the risk-control system. The feature platform computes the tabular features of the current transaction, retrieves the preceding user, card, and device histories, and looks up the latest eligible graph embedding of the user. History retrieval typically 6 takes 5060 ms. The model service encodes the assembled inputs and returns risk score. The strategy platform combines the score with the active rules and intervention budget and returns the risk decision. The complete workflow must finish within 250 ms end-to-end budget, which covers feature access, model-service communication and inference, and the final decision (Figure 2). model-service budget: 120 ms Feature platform tabular features, histories, graph-embedding lookup Model service (A10) encoders, fusion, experts, risk head Strategy platform score, rules, intervention budget history retrieval: 5060 ms mean 46.66 ms P99 80.16 ms payment event time risk decision end-to-end budget: 250 ms Figure 2 Online scoring timeline of Antom 3-in-1 Transformer. Latencies are monitored values; braces mark service budgets. Stage widths are schematic. Inference performance. The model service runs on an NVIDIA A10 GPU under 120 ms service budget. Online monitoring records mean latency of 46.66 ms, P95 of 55.86 ms, and P99 of 80.16 ms.

sections.title: 4.4 Foundation Model Capabilities
sections.content: We examine how pretrained foundation reduces the labels needed for new business, transfers to other business scenarios and explore how the foundation model could benefit other tasks. Low-label adaptation. To evaluate label efficiency, we fine-tune the pretrained model and the same architecture trained from scratch with 1%, 5%, 10%, 25%, and 100% of the training labels, keeping the validation set fixed. With 25% of the labels, the pretrained model already exceeds scratch training with all labels on both Antom-Merchant and Antom-Merchant (Figure 3). On AntomMerchant A, it reaches 0.5246% AP and 8.33% R@0.5%, against 0.4205% and 7.81% for full-label scratch; on Antom-Merchant B, it reaches 0.6928% and 10.16%, against 0.6370% and 8.11%. Pretraining also flattens the label curve: with 25% of the labels, the pretrained model retains 87% of its full-label recall on Antom-Merchant and 71% on Antom-Merchant B, compared with 73% and 62% for scratch training. HK is the most label-scarce business, with 732 positive training examples, so we evaluate it at 10% and 100% of the labels only. With 10% of the labels, the pretrained model reaches 0.8214% AP and 27.75% R@0.5%, well above scratch training with all labels (0.1148% and 10.41%). Across the evaluated budgets, pretraining improves both metrics over same-budget scratch on HK and Antom-Merchant B. Cross-scenario application. To evaluate the cross-scenario capability, we first fine-tune pretrained model on target business whose histories were excluded from pretraining. The pretrained model and its scratch counterpart share the architecture, target labels, fine-tuning budget, and selection rule. Pretraining improves the target business metric by 34.5% and AUROC by 0.0518 over scratch. The gain does not depend on few risk-dense accounts: after removing the accounts with the highest concentration of risk events, the business-metric gain remains 34.2%. 7 Figure 3 Label efficiency on Antom-Merchant and Antom-Merchant B. Points and error bars show the mean and standard deviation over three fine-tuning runs. We then test how the pretraining data source affects transfer. Three checkpoints of the same size and budget are pretrained on Antom-Merchant histories only, on Antom-Merchant histories only, and on an equal mixture of both. Each checkpoint is fine-tuned on each target business with 10% or 25% of its labels  (Table 4)  . Pretraining only on the other business already improves AP and R@0.5% over scratch in all four targetbudget settings. For Antom-Merchant with 10% labels, Antom-Merchant histories help even more than Antom-Merchant Bs own (0.5791% vs. 0.4857% AP; 8.67% vs. 6.13% R@0.5%). Histories in the Antom-Merchant cohort are shorter on average, with 7.8 events compared with 29.5 for Antom-Merchant A. Thus, richer histories from another scenario can partly substitute for in-domain ones. With 25% labels, mixing the two sources beats target-only pretraining on both metrics for both targets. Besides risk assessment, Antom 3-in-1 Transformer serves payment routing tasks. The payment routing tasks purpose is to route each payment to suitable channels and improve the payment success rate (PSR). By post-training on payment routing tasks, we found that Antom 3-in-1 Transformer improves PSR by 2.16% relative to our internal deployed model. Antom 3-in-1 Transformer allows requests containing both risk and payment routing features to detect transaction risk and improve PSR.

sections.title: 4.5 Modality Pretraining and Fusion Results

We compare PFC with CoLES, BYB, and CPC using the same encoder, pretraining data, and training budget  (Table 5)  . PFC achieves the best AP and R@0.5% across all three evaluation domains at both label budgets. With 10% of the HK labels, it reaches 0.8214% AP and 27.75% R@0.5%, compared with 0.0342% and 3.31% for scratch training. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed methods across sequence pretraining, graph augmentation, and expert fusion. PFC improves downstream performance under limited supervision by learning informative sequence representations, TGRF introduces complementary relational information to strengthen risk prediction, and task-attention based expert fusion further improves detection performance through adaptive expert weighting, particularly at low intervention budgets. The consistent gains across diverse datasets, label budgets, and evaluation settings provide further evidence of the effectiveness and robustness of our proposed framework.

sections.title: 4.7 Case Study
sections.content: We inspect whether pretrained representations distinguish payment behaviors and how individual histories occupy the learned representation space. Evasion and account nurturing. Evasion changes payment resources or attempt timing to get past risk controls, while account nurturing builds routine-looking activity before later misuse. The pretrained representations of these two groups form two largely separated regions in PCA. We inspect 2,880 annotated histories, including both risk patterns and legitimate histories with similar behavior, and visualize their representations with PCA and t-SNE (Figure 4). The region contains 374 histories and is dominated by evasion-type histories. Behavior pattern case study. Samples in the outlined region of Figure 4 show typical behavior pattern, rapidly retrying at the same merchant. Figure 5 details the pattern. Among 361 annotated feedbackadjustment pairs in the region, 95.6% retain the same merchant, compared with 70.7% among 916 pairs outside the surrounding island. Median intervals are 4.8 minutes and 22.8 hours, respectively. After rejection, the example changes the card while retaining the device and IP address. After another rejection, both card and device change while the IP address stays. sections.title: 5.1 Transaction Risk Modeling
sections.content: Transaction risk models have moved from hand-crafted features toward sequential and graphbased learning. Early systems feed manually designed statistics, such as velocity features, into tabular learners such as gradient-boosted trees (Chen and Guestrin, 2016; Prokhorenkova et al., 2018). Later work models transaction histories directly with sequential networks (Jurgovsky et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2023b), or connects accounts, devices, and merchants into graphs and applies graph neural networks (Dou et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2021, 2018; Tang et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2019). Recent advances in large language models have spurred the development of transaction foundation models (Dou et al., 2025; Ostroukhov et al., 2026).

sections.title: 5.2 Pretrained Transaction Foundation Models
sections.content: Transaction pretraining uses two main forms of supervision: event reconstruction learns dependencies among heterogeneous fields through masking or next-event prediction, as in TabBERT, FATATrans, TransactionGPT, and PRAGMA (Dou et al., 2025; Ostroukhov et al., 2026; Padhi et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2023b); temporal learning instead relates segments of history: CoLES contrasts subsequences, while CPC and BYB predict future representations (Babaev et al., 2022; van den Oord et al., 2018; Wu et al., 2025). Transaction foundation models extend these objectives with profile 12 information and reusable representations for multiple business tasks (Li et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2026). Despite their achievements in transaction modeling, they mainly capture transaction features from single perspective. Antom 3-in-1 Transformer uses three modalities to provide more comprehensive view of transactions.

sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: We presented Antom 3-in-1 Transformer, payment foundation model applied on billion-scale industrial payment systems, which combines transaction sequences, scenario-specific tabular features, and entity relationships for card-payment risk. Sequence modality captures behavioral evolution, tabular modality models contextual feature interactions, and graph modality learns structure of user relationships. Antom 3-in-1 Transformer has been deployed on Ant Internationals industrial system since June 2026 and reduces overall loss rate by 37.88% relative to current internal fraud detection system. Antom 3-in-1 Transformer demonstrates promising generalization capabilities across diverse scenarios and tasks. The technologies developed in this work have also strengthened Ant Internationals overall risk management capabilities.
